questions.question: Pentane boils at 36,1 °C, 2-methylbutane at 27,8 °C and 2,2-dimethylpropane at 9,5 °C, yet all three have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂. Explain this trend fully, using the four-step structure for property explanations.
questions.expected_answer: Step one, structural difference: the three compounds are chain isomers differing only in branching — pentane is unbranched, 2-methylbutane has one methyl branch, 2,2-dimethylpropane has two branches on the same carbon and is the most compact. Step two, forces: all three are nonpolar alkanes, so the only intermolecular forces are London (dispersion) forces. Step three, comparison: London forces act over the surface of contact between molecules. Straight pentane chains can lie alongside each other and attract along their whole length; branching makes the molecule more compact and nearly spherical, reducing the surface area of contact between neighbouring molecules, so the dispersion forces weaken as branching increases. Step four, energy: weaker intermolecular forces need less energy to overcome, so the boiling point falls as branching increases — from 36,1 °C for the straight chain to 9,5 °C for the most branched isomer. Molar mass cannot explain the trend, since all three isomers have identical molecular formulae and masses.

questions.question: Butane (M = 58 g·mol⁻¹, boiling point −0,5 °C), propanal (M = 58 g·mol⁻¹, boiling point 48,8 °C) and propan-1-ol (M = 60 g·mol⁻¹, boiling point 97,2 °C) have nearly equal molar masses. Explain the differences in boiling point, and predict with a reason where propanoic acid would fit.
questions.expected_answer: Because the molar masses are nearly equal, the London forces are of similar strength in all three, so the differences come from the functional groups. Butane is a nonpolar alkane with only London forces between its molecules — the weakest total attraction, hence the lowest boiling point. Propanal is an aldehyde: its carbonyl group makes the molecule polar, so dipole-dipole forces act in addition to London forces; the stronger total attraction needs more energy to overcome, raising the boiling point to 48,8 °C. Propan-1-ol is an alcohol: its OH group has hydrogen bonded directly to oxygen, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds — the strongest intermolecular force here — and the boiling point rises to 97,2 °C. Propanoic acid would boil higher than all three (it boils at about 141 °C): the carboxyl group hydrogen-bonds at two sites, and pairs of acid molecules clasp each other in a double hydrogen bond (dimers), giving the strongest intermolecular attraction of the four and therefore requiring the most energy to separate the molecules.

questions.question: Define vapour pressure, state its relationship to intermolecular force strength and boiling point, and use it to explain why an ester can be smelled across a room while propan-1-ol evaporates slowly from an open beaker.
questions.expected_answer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid that is in equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container. It is inversely related to intermolecular force strength: strong intermolecular forces hold molecules in the liquid so few escape, giving a low vapour pressure and a high boiling point; weak intermolecular forces allow many molecules to escape, giving a high vapour pressure and a low boiling point — a volatile liquid. (A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.) Esters have dipole-dipole and London forces between their molecules but cannot hydrogen-bond with one another, so their intermolecular forces are relatively weak; their vapour pressure is comparatively high, many molecules escape into the air, and those airborne molecules reach your nose — which is why fruity ester smells travel and why esters are used in flavourings and perfumes. Propan-1-ol's molecules are held by hydrogen bonds, the strongest intermolecular force in the syllabus, so far fewer molecules escape per second: a lower vapour pressure, slower evaporation, and a higher boiling point.
